title: AI-AUGMENTED HAZARD DETECTION AND AVOIDANCE FOR THE L4 ENCELADUS LANDER - EXPRO+
description: ObjectivesAssess the feasibility of using physics-based granular dynamics simulation to model the formation of cryovolcanic terrains on Enceladus and derive insights into surface compactness. Develop a proof-of-concept ML model for inferring snow/ice geophysicalproperties (e.g., density, snow water equivalent) by correlating terrestrial in-situ scientific data with satellite remote sensing observations. Initiate the adaptation of classical, optimization-based HDA frameworks to integrate AIderived geophysical safety maps, establishing a baseline for a future hybrid HDA architecture. Conduct an extensive performance and resource consumption benchmark of key AI and HDA software components on representative space-grade hardware, establishing the trade-space between algorithmic capability and on-board computational budgetDescriptionThe ESA Voyage 2050 L4 mission to Enceladus requires an autonomous landing in the South Polar Terrain to achieve its core astrobiological objectives. This environment presents unique challenges that transcend classical HDA capabilities. Landing hazardsare not only geometric (e.g., slopes, rocks), but also geophysical. Due to the unknown load-bearing capacity of cryovolcanic surface deposits, landing sites can appear perfectly flat and clear of hazards and yet be catastrophically unsafe. Classical existing Hazard Detection and Avoidance (HDA) frameworks targeting Moon and Mars, are highly mature for geometric hazard assessment but are not designed to infer subsurface geophysical properties from remote sensing data. This activity shall address this critical technology gap by investigating the integration of AI/ML-based geophysicalinference into a proven HDA decision-making architecture. Additionally, the severe power and computational constraints of a solar-powered missionto Saturn imposea hard limit on the complexity of on-board AI. It is currently unknown what level of "intelligence" is achievable within a realistic resource budget. This activity shall perform the foundational trade-off analysis required to inform mission designers of the necessary hardware and power provisions for a reliable and capable AI-augmented HDA system

title: MATURATION OF ZERO BOIL OFF COMPONENTS (RTB CRYOCOOLER) OF LIQUID OXYGEN (LOX) - EXPRO+
description: Objective:  To design and develop a cryocooler breadboard model, based on the Reverse Turbo-Brayton, targeting LOx temperature, for the long duration storage of liquid cryogenic propellants for in Space application. Description:  Cryogenic propellants are being considered and baselined for future missions as a valid alternative to storable propellants for orbital and deep space missions.A combination of Liquid Oxygen (LOX) and Liquid cryogenic propellants provide significant advantages in term of performance over storable fuel and oxidizers.  Several classes of orbital and deep space missions can benefit from cryogenic propulsion systems. However, cryogenic propulsion systems technologies are only available for short duration missions (max. 1 day, launchers). Extending the operating life of these systems requires a range of new technologies, more adapted to high volume transfer at lower pressure, andfor a long-time duration of operations and long cycles in space (days to weeks).  Handling cryogenic fluid in space for long duration necessitates the introduction of a so called Zero Boil off systems where active cooling systems are needed.  In order to increase TRL for such system and especially for the cryocooler part, this activity targets to design, manufacture a testing model and perform test under representative environment on ground, targeting the LOx temperature range, of around 90K, coinciding also with sub-cooled LCH4, and would also demonstrate the first technological bricks for a LH2 RTB cryocooler of such size. Also the heat lifts is targeted to be in the range of 100-200W, which is considered an important stepping stone into enabling zero boil-off components storage in-orbit of cryogenic propellants.   This activity encompasses the following tasks:   - - - - Requirements definition, design trade-offs, a development plan, industrial plan (incl. make or buy analyses) to reach TRL4 at the end of the activity at component level, A systems sizing exercise (considering ZBO LOX tank application), and the associated detailed design of the 90K Class RTB Breadboard Test plan, HW manufacturing and testing Test results exploitation, lessons learned and recommendations for future or complementary development Deliverables: Breadboard, Report

title: CRYOCOOLER ELECTRONICS DEMONSTRATION MODEL VERSATILE FOR MEDIUM CATEGORY CRYOCOOLER - EXPRO+
description: Objective: To develop a versatile demonstration model of Cryocooler Electronics, suitable for a Medium Category Cryocooler.Description: Availability of an off-the-shelf Cryocooler Electronics that is versatile, affordable and readily available could decrease the costs and schedule risks of payloads requiring cryocooled focal planes. Cryocooler Units (CCU) - the full cryocooler delivered assembly - rely on a driver unit called "Cryocooler Electronics" (CCE) that has multiple control functions, such as providing and regulating electrical power, temperature control, micro-vibrations control and launch locking. These CCEs tend to be custom-made for eachcryocooler and mission due to specific needs, such as the cryocooler nature itself, its operating principle, the electrical input power range, bus power interfaces, TM/TC protocol, and other requirements. This bespoke nature makes the CCE a driver in the cryocooler's deliverable critical path and an important barrier to overall Cryocooler Unit affordability. The activity conducts a review of the most relevant use cases, such as Earth Observation optical instrument focal plane cooling, low-earth orbit constellations requiring cryocooling, and space science observatories. The review shall result with identified the main interface requirements and designdrivers that can lead to differentiated CCE designs. The most promising set of interface and functional requirements shall be selected that will render the Versatile CCE with the broadest cross-cutting compatibility across said platforms. Following this a CCE demonstration model design is manufactured and tested. The activity encompasses the following tasks: - Reviewing and setting the requirements applicable to the Cryocooler Electronics, referring to multiple use cases and cryocooler natures in the 60W class; - CCE design and breadboard tests - CCE demonstration model manufacturing - CCE demonstration model testing - Way forward for industrialisationDeliverables: Breadboard, Report

title: SUSTAINABLE 3D-PRINTED ACTIVE AND PASSIVE RF COMPONENTS FOR ANTENNA ARRAY APPLICATIONS - EXPRO+
description: Objective:To develop and demonstrate 3D-printed active and passive RF components for L-band antenna arrayapplications, enabling more sustainable manufacturing and system integration.Description:The environmental impact of space activities is receiving increasing attention across the European spacesector. In line with ESA's Ecodesign Policy, future missions are expected to assess their environmentalfootprint through Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) and identify and implement solutions that reduce resourceconsumption, energy usage, waste generation, and hazardous materials. RF hardware is a particularly relevant target for ecodesign improvements due to its widespread deployment across satellite payloads and user terminals. Given the large number of RF components typically integrated within phased-array antenna architectures, even incremental reductions in environmental impacts at component level can translate into significant cumulative benefits at system and programme level.Phased Array Antennas (PAAs) are a key enabling technology for next-generation communications,navigation, and sensing systems, providing electronically steerable beams, enhanced reliability, andoperational flexibility. Conventional PAA manufacturing relies on complex and resource-intensive productionprocesses. Additive manufacturing, and in particular 3D printing, offers a sustainable alternative approachthrough the use of functional polymers and carbon-nanotube-based materials while reducing waste, energyusage, water consumption, and chemical processing.While significant progress has been achieved for passive RF components, the development of active RFdevices, particularly RF transistors, remains a key challenge and a barrier to fully 3D-printed RF systems. The ESA Discovery activity "GHz Organic Printed Transistors" (GHioza) demonstrated sustainable 3D-printed transistor technology up to approximately 300 MHz which is state of the art but not sufficient for phase-array antenna applications. The activity aims to develop sustainably manufactured 3D-printed RF transistorsoperating in L-band (1-2 GHz) and integrate them with antenna elements on a common substrate,demonstrating the co-integration of active and passive RF functionality within a unified additively manufacturedplatform. A proof-of-concept active array demonstrator comprising two to three antenna elements andassociated active circuitry will then be developed, with electronic beam steering demonstrated using anexternal Software Defined Radio for beamforming and phase control.This activity encompasses the following tasks:- requirements analysis- material characterization- RF transistor design- antenna/component co-integration- additive manufacturing process development- prototype fabrication- RF testing and validation- beam-steering demonstrations- development plan- Simplified LCA analysis and Ecodesign trade off and selection.Procurement Policy: C(1) = Activity restricted to non-prime contractors (incl. SMEs).
